paragraph.text: B16. "It's a fair trade: we care for them and feed them, and they give us meat"
the idea of an agreement between humans and farmed animals, defended in books such as Stephen Budiansky's

(1992), assumes a trade. But a trade requires that both parties can accept or refuse, and the animal can't. The same side that "protects" is the one that kills, and the price charged is life itself, in a fraction of the time the animal could have lived. The fact that the species multiplied through domestication doesn't benefit each individual born to be slaughtered. And the most serious academic version, J. Baird Callicott's "domestication contract", condemns intensive farming, where almost all meat comes from.
"We give them food, shelter, protect them from predators and care for them when they're sick. In return, they give us meat. It's a fair deal, and nature is much worse."
Farmed animals receive food, shelter, protection from predators and veterinary care.
In the wild, they would suffer from hunger, disease and predators.
A relationship in which each side gives something and receives something is a fair trade.
So breeding animals and killing them for food is a fair trade.

P1 is partly true, and depends a lot on the farming system. P2 compares with an alternative that isn't on the table: these animals wouldn't live in the wild, they simply wouldn't be bred. P3 is false when one side can neither consent nor refuse.
"We care for them, they give us meat. It's a trade."
"Out there they'd be eaten by another animal."
"There's a pact between the farmer and the animal."
"Domestication was a successful evolutionary strategy for these species."
"Without farming, these animals wouldn't even exist." (which is B7)

A trade is when both sides agree, like swapping stickers. The cow didn't agree to anything: nobody asked her, and she can't say no. And in the end, the one who cared for her is the one who takes her life. That isn't a trade, it's a decision made by only one side.

A fair trade requires that both sides can accept or refuse, and the animal can't. The one who "protects" is the same one who kills, and the price is life itself, charged long before its natural end. Would you accept a deal in which the other side decides everything and you pay with your life? And if the species multiplied through domestication, that doesn't help the individual born to be slaughtered. And comparing with nature doesn't help: without farming, these animals wouldn't be out there suffering; they wouldn't have been bred.
"If it were a fair trade, could the animal say no?"

An agreement in which only one side sets the terms, and the other can neither accept nor refuse, isn't a trade. Between humans, we'd call it an imposition.
The argument describes the farmer as the one who protects the animal, but the farmer is the one who kills them. Protecting someone in order to kill them later isn't protection; it's breeding for use.
What the animal "pays" is their life, usually long before its natural end. No care received beforehand makes up for losing everything that would have come after.
Domestication multiplied the numbers of cattle, pigs and chickens, but that doesn't benefit each animal who is born. It is the individual who feels, not the species (see A10).
Without farming, these animals wouldn't be roaming free and suffering from predators; they simply wouldn't be bred (see B7).

text.bold: 6. If there's a trade, animals contribute, and then they count.

paragraph.text: A common objection to justice for animals, tied to John Rawls's idea of reciprocity, says they don't contribute to society and so aren't entitled to what it distributes. The fair-trade argument concedes the opposite: animals give meat, milk, eggs, wool and labor. The political philosopher Alasdair Cochrane notes that animals on farms, in laboratories and in homes are part of how society functions, and that by the contribution criterion they should be included in justice (Cochrane, 2010, p. 56). Whoever accepts the trade can't also say they give nothing (see A21 and A25).

(d) The strongest counter-reply: the domestication contract
The most serious version says that at the start of domestication, some animals approached humans of their own accord, because they gained food and protection, and that this shows a kind of consent.

The environmental philosopher J. Baird Callicott gave this idea an academic form: by bringing animals into a "mixed community" with humans, we would have entered an implicit contract with them. Under the contract, we may use and even slaughter them, provided we give them proper pastoral care. Callicott himself concludes that intensive farming breaches this contract and is therefore wrong.
The journalist Michael Pollan gave the idea its most widely read version, in a
essay that replies directly to Peter Singer ("An Animal's Place", 2002), taken up again in

(2006). Pollan says domestication was an evolutionary process, not a political one: some species discovered, by Darwinian trial and error, that they prospered more in alliance with humans, and calling it domination would project a human idea of power onto what is in fact mutualism between species. Cattle, pigs and chickens multiplied, while their wild relatives declined. For Pollan, a species can have interests, and a domesticated animal's good lies in expressing its own nature, which, for these species, doesn't happen apart from humans. He grants that industrial farming is an evil and that, faced with it, vegetarianism is a reasonable response; but he concludes that the wrong lies in the practice, not the principle, and points, as a model, to farms such as Joel Salatin's Polyface, in Virginia, where each species lives according to its own nature.

It's true that many farmers feed and care for their animals, that life in the wild involves a lot of suffering, and that domestication multiplied these species.
But a trade requires that both sides can refuse, and the price charged is the animal's life. Caring for someone doesn't give the right to kill them.
